utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. This is Wednesday, February 6, 2008, and I welcome the representatives from Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, and all the people helping us in this courtroom. Regarding procedure now, I have a few items. First thing tomorrow the hearing will start at 8.30. The registrar was told about it. So we will start at 8.30 a.m., and we will run till 1.15 p.m., and we will be in Courtroom III. I will ask Mr. Registrar to move into closed session because we have two decisions to render and we need closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. This has to do with the motion, Prosecution motion, to add 55 documents to the 65 ter list filed on December 24, 2007, and these are documents that were included in the Theunens report. Yesterday, I dealt with this, but I believe that we have to rediscuss this issue because there are a few things I need to add. Yesterday the accused obtained the translation in his own language of the Prosecution's motion. During yesterday's hearing, Mr. Seselj, you told us that you didn't have time to study this motion and look into it. Now we have the following problem: Do you want to answer and reply to this motion? Remember that the witness is scheduled to be -- to testify next week. If you tell us you know verbally that you have read the motion and that you have no objection to adding these 55 documents to the 65 ter list, or if you actually object to this, then the Trial Chamber will be able to rule very quickly on this, before the witness is actually called next week. So what's your position regarding this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I oppose that motion in principle in a manner that will not bring into question the scheduling of Witness Theunens' testimony. The Prosecution engaged this expert witness several years ago. They had these documents at their disposal. They could have found them earlier. They waited for the last moment. In my view this is unacceptable. However, if my objection or written motion would bring into question the scheduling of lawyer Theunens' testimony, then I will waive my objection. I believe Your Honour should reprimand the Prosecution, but I do not want to obstruct the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So verbally you're telling us that in you're in opposition in principle, backing this by the fact that the Prosecution had time to do this and did this at the very last minute, and this is what you oppose. Further -- but on the other hand you do not want to postpone the calling of this expert witness, so if the Chamber rules to dismiss your opposition to this motion then you can start cross-examination next week. Is this what you actually wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You understand me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, I have one final topic to address. This is an order to clarify the two motions of the Prosecution dealing with the judicial notice of documentary evidence issued by the Trial Chamber yesterday on February 5, 2008. Yesterday in its decision, the Chamber ordered Prosecution to clarify its two motions requesting judicial notice of exhibits, asking it to provide additional details, notably as to the relevance and to the description of the documents involved. The Trial Chamber notes that the accused has already answered to these two motions on the judicial notice of exhibits. However, Trial Chamber would like to remind Mr. Seselj that if he wishes to, he can reply to this -- to the clarification made by Prosecution within the 14 days' time limit which is provided for Rule 126 bis. So let me sum this up. As you know, Mr. Seselj, Prosecution filed two motions for the Trial Chamber to establish judicial notice of documentary evidence which had already been admitted in other proceedings, in other cases. The Chamber ruled yesterday, so you didn't obtain a translation in B/C/S; but it was asking the Prosecution to provide additional information on these documents regarding the relevance of these documents, the description of these documents, the relationship of these documents to the indictment and so on. Now, the Prosecution is going to reply to our request in writing, and when replying in writing you will be able to give us your opinion on this, and you will have two weeks, 14 days, as of the moment when you receive in your own language the reply made by the Prosecution. Have you understood this? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I categorically oppose this also. The fact that another Trial Chamber admitted certain documents does not mean anything to you in principle in this trial. There the Judges had other motives. The situation was different. The confrontation between the Prosecution and the Defence was different. There, perhaps, the Defence did not oppose such motions, so something might have been admitted automatically. There is no reason for the Prosecution not to tender these documents in one of two ways in this trial. One is through the witness testimony, and the other by tendering the documents directly as they have already done with a number of exhibits I have not yet expressed my standpoint about. And then that could be the fate of these documents also. If the Prosecution feels that it's an argument in their favour, namely that another Trial Chamber has admitted the documents, they are wrong. It means nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have understood your position, and it's extremely clear. So when the Prosecution will file his reply and when you will obtain it in your own language, you will have two -- 14 days as of that moment. If you don't answer on my [as interpreted] 19 page 6 until line 9 page 7, we will have your official position regarding this issue. So this is now on the transcript. Let's now bring the witness into the courtroom, we will proceed with the cross-examination. As soon as the witness will be in the witness seat, I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination. I believe that you have about two hours and 15 minutes left. Let me ask Mr. Registrar and the legal officer to confirm this, and I will tell you exactly how long you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Please be seated. Very well. Good afternoon. The cross-examination is going to be continued. Mr. Seselj, you have two hours and 25 minutes left. You have the floor, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, we will now go in detail through this allegedly expert report of yours. In the introduction which is on page 4 in the Serbian translation, you claim that the Serbian medieval state came into existence in the Raska region. You therefore do not where and when the first Serbian state came into existence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 10th century there were several Serbian states. They were mentioned by Constantine the 7th in Verozinet [phoen]. He was the emperor. He mentioned Nurdjana as its name, Travunija, Konavlje, the state of Duklja as well, as well as a Serbian state headed by Ceslav. Therefore, however, Serb historians are of the view that the true Serbian state that is going to develop throughout history starts with Stefan Nemanja, late 12th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which Serbian historian considers that the true Serbian state begins with Stefan Nemanja? Give me his first and last name?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The history of Serbs of Vladimir Corovic, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't read that in Vladimir Corovic. You just think you did. The first Serbian state came into existence as early as the 9th century. You mentioned Constantine. I assume you understand his nickname was Porphyrogenitus, and he was an historian. You didn't mention his nickname which is very significant. Do you know that the Serbian Neretian state, what territory did it take up?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previous answer, that's what I said earlier on. Present answer. This small state was at the level of the Neretva River, the mouth of the Neretva River. This state was known for its piracy activities. The pirates of that state were very active in the Adriatic Sea being an obstacle at the time to trade in Venicia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Neretva was the southern border of that Serbian state. What was its northern border, do you know?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it is held that the boundary between the Serb and Croat populations between the state of Nerevnja [phoen] and the Croatian state was the Cetina river further north.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The river Cetina by the town of Omis not far from Split, is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Indeed, further north of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. Mr. Tomic, you should have included that in your expert report then. Do you know on what territory the Hum state extended, the Hum Serbian state, also mentioned by Constantine Porphyrogenitus as Serbian?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hum state the region of Herzegovina did not exist. We had Zahumlje as a state at the time. There was also Travunija that corresponds to the Trebinje area. Hum as a state would gather all these territories later, but that name appeared only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you ought to know that the Hum state and Zahumlje are one in the same thing. It's just a variation in the name whereas the Travunija is a separate Serbian state. On what territory did the Serb state of Travunija extend?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly around the town, the present town of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All the way to Boka Kotorska; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you go further south you have a small state, the state of Konavlje south of Dubrovnik, basically, right to the mouth of Kotor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Konavlje was a Serbian princedom; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the case against Constantine VII. These are small principalities, states, that are regarded as Serbian states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you recall, Constantine Porphyrogenitus said clearly that these were in fact autonomous princedoms subordinated to the Archon of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you read the original by Constantine Porphyrogenitus?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Breaks between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the work?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read the original. However, I read books on the history of the Middle Ages that referred to this document because this is one of the rare documents providing information on the breakdown of peoples in the area. This document is known as being "administrando imperio."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, the Gretile [phoen] was about peoples, so there are two different titles that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You left out one thing because you didn't read the original by Constantine Porphyrogenitus. He speaks of the Serb state, the Neretva state which he even calls Pagania because that's where the Serbs were baptised latest and then Humska, Zahumlje, Travunija, Konavlje, Diokvija [phoen] or the Duklja state. However, in the background of all these Serbian lands Constantine Trebinje said was the real Serbia. These were all autonomous parts of that one single Serbia. You don't know of these details, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides all these small principalities, I mentioned the state of Serbia. Ruled by Caslav, but the boundaries of that state were not known in any detail. In history books, the boundaries of that state are mentioned, but indeed they were not known in any detail towards the mid-10th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know when Caslav restored the Serbian state, in what year?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 930, but I'm not a specialist in the history of the Middle Ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know enough. It was in 927. So you're not far off the mark. But why was it necessary to restore the Serbian state at the time of Caslav? What was it that happened before Caslav? Who conquered the Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time the Byzantine Empire played a major part in the Balkan Peninsula, but you also have the Bulgarian state but at the time extended to a large part of the peninsula up to the area populated by Croats in the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just before the end of the 9th century, Mr. Tomic, Bulgarians conquered all Serbian lands and the Serbian state stopped to exist for a while until 927 when it was restored by Caslav, and he managed to restore the Serbian state because Bulgarians were pushed back by Byzantine. Those are basics that you should have learned. Why am I saying this? Isn't it quite obvious from all of this that if these were Serbian lands, the Neretva state, Zahumlje, Travunija, Konavlje and Duklja, and if behind them there is Serbia, the Serbian population lived there. Isn't that clear?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indicated in the document by Constantine VII at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the first historical source mentioning Serbs in the Balkans, the most ancient source?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the most ancient documents there are chronicles coming from the Franks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what is the name of the chronicle, Frankish chronicle?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the chronicle exists, but I don't know the name of its writer. I didn't study this period in any detail. I know the chronicle exists because the Franks controlled the territory that is today Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Franks controlled Croatian territory and it stretched from the river Cetina until north towards mount Gvozd that was the first Croatian state, correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the 9th century, yes, but later on that territory or state will expand under Tomislav in the first half of the 10th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Up to what point did it stretch until -- under Tomislav?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extended to the Panonia Plain but also included territory that now represents Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean to say the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but one thing is certain, this state experienced a vast expansion at the time. At the time, the boundaries of states kept moving, evolving, depending on the conflicts or as a result of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you know who was the best Croatian connoisseur of medieval history, especially Croatian history, his name, a renowned Croatian historian?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One Klaic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Klaic is from 19th century. I'm speaking about modern times. Nada Klaic, university professor in Zagreb. She's the best Croatian historian for the Middle Ages, and she established that the Croatian state stretched from Cetina river to Mount Gvodza that it stretched in this period up to behind Livno and north to the Sava River. And when did the Croatian state have the largest borders, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the 11th century under King Petar Kresimir IV. It reached until Vrbas river in the east, in the north nobody knows for sure. They say up to Drava River, directly to the Drava River through Croatian Zagorje. You don't know that, therefore you know very little about medieval history?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please avoid testifying yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not testifying, Madam Judge, I'm just letting the witness know certain facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but you are presently testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can deprive me of the right to examine the witness. You can do anything. But I'm trying to prove to you that this witness knows nothing and at best his knowledge is very superficial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, nobody wants to prevent you from asking questions. However, as you know, these are Anglo-Saxon proceedings. As part of cross-examination you're supposed to ask questions. You're not supposed be a witness yourself. Therefore, what you should have said is this: In the 11th century, if I were to tell you that it is King Petar Kresimir IV, would you agree would me or not? The witness can then answer that he agrees with you or doesn't, and then you can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quite fair, Mr. President, if I tell the witness you don't know that the Croatian state was the largest under King Petar Kresimir IV and that it encompassed this and that. That is a completely fair question in this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know under what church authorities Serbs were in the first centuries of their existence in the Balkan Peninsula?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under what church authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it was all Christian faith. There was no -- there was no split in the church. There were various archbishopries. That was the only division to which our archbishopries did the Serbs belong in the medieval times?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly as to this precise period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that Serbs were in the Split and Drac archbishopries. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not research into the history of the church. I know that the Serbian church was created in 1219 by Sveti Sava, St. Sava. As of that period there was an Orthodox Serbian church that was created and will expand towards the territories along the Dalmatian coast. That is where bishopries were going to be created. There were only two of them back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you don't know church issues, and that's why you are unable to write a quality expert report, because you don't know the essential problem, the church problem, in the relations between Serbs and Croat. You don't know that, do you? You're talking about St. Sava, who appeared 200 years later. Centuries mean nothing to you, do they?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know parts of the church history, but my report was not focusing on this. It was focusing on the 19th and the 20th century, whilst you are now going into detail into the Middle Ages, which is quite remote even though the church dimension was a relevant one at a time when national identities were going to be more strong in the 19th century. But in my report I was not supposed to deal with the division of the territory into bishopries in the 9th or the 10th centuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One clarification. Your title is "The Greater Serbian Ideology in the 19th and 20th Centuries." That's the title of your expert report. That was the focus of your report. It may be that the witness should have gone back to the 9th century, maybe, but apparently that was not his remit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you have an introduction to this report which claims to provide basic information about the latest Serbian history in the Balkans. The entire report abounds in claims of this alleged expert that Serbs are Orthodox Christians, whereas Croats are Catholics. I'm trying to prove that the witness doesn't know anything about this, that Serbs belong to two archbishopries, out of which one belonged to the split which was cast Catholic, and the other was Orthodox, Drac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that Serbian populations especially from the Uklja [phoen] region that was later to be called Zeta was under the influence of the Catholic church at least until the 12th century Mihailo, who was the King of the Zeta or Uklja state who was crowned by the Pope in the year 1077. That was after the schism of 1054, and the founder of Nemanjic dynasty Stefan Nemanja was from that region, and he was first baptised as Catholic, but later on he was rebaptised once he became King in -- he was rebaptised in the Orthodox church in Raska. At the time the Serbian populations of the various regional units were divided depending on their religion, either Catholic or Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the accused is criticising your report, and therefore I would like to put a question to you. The scope of your report was the Greater Serbia ideology in the 19th and 20th centuries, and I find that you do not really deal with the topic of religion. Is it something that you did on purpose not to deal with that particular topic, or did you think that it was totally irrelevant to deal with the topic of Catholic, Orthodox, the impact of religion on writings, on ideology, and so on and so forth? Is this deliberate on your part, or did you estimate that it was totally irrelevant and useless? Because what the accused is trying to do is to put this into another perspective, in a religious perspective. He's going back to the 19th, 10th, 11th, and 12th century because -- it's because according to him, and of course the Chamber will have to rule on it later on, it's because according to him this is indeed very relevant, but why did you choose not to deal with the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's because in the main documents where the programme for a Greater Serbia in the 19th century is being formulated, this topic is not raised or dealt with, because at the time the notion of language was much more relevant than the topic of religion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I understand what you mean. I would like to know whether you had the opportunity to read some of the works by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wrote more than 80 books in total. Did you read or see any of the books where he challenges the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, but these books were published after the year 2000, including the book on the ideology of Serb nationalism, a book dealing with the artificial nature of the Croatian state with the criticism of the Vatican. I am a historian. I am interested in chronology and what -- I was interested in were the ideas of Mr. Seselj as they evolved throughout the 1980s and throughout the years of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. What was drafted or written later on by him, of course, can be relevant; but this was not directly relevant to the period I was interested in. You cannot work without historical perspective. That's why I decided to focus on what he had written in the years 1980s and between 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to let you and your colleagues know first of all that I'm trying to refute the theory of the expert that Serbs are Orthodox and Croats are Catholic. I'm trying to show through this debate that before St. Sava, the overwhelming majority of Serbs belonged to the Roman Catholic Church. That is the point, the main point, and I believe that is very important to my concept of Greater Serbia even though other people may not advocate it in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not said anything contrary to that. I said that at least to the 12th century what we can call the Serb world populated by Serbs was a region where you found Orthodox to the east and more to the west along the Adriatic sea. Catholics, Roman Catholics. But later on the Orthodox church expanded to -- towards the regions located next to the coast, and Catholic Serbs became Orthodox later on. But up until the 20th century, there remained a population that is not very significant but a population of Serbs who see them receives, well, Catholics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is not in contradiction with what Mr. Seselj told us earlier year on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any difference between what we say. I said that this was valid until the 20th -- 12th century. Later on, once the patriarch of the Serb Orthodox Church was reinstated between 12th -- 1257 and later on, the area of expansion was quite significant, and when bishopries were created and churches were built in areas where you didn't used to have any Orthodox churches before. Along the coast you have an area under the influence of the Roman Catholic Church, but throughout the Ottoman period, we find that the Orthodox church gets stronger, grows stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this period we are discussing, Mr. Tomic, there were no inter-religious animosities. There was no opposition, confrontation between Catholic and Orthodox people. There is no historical source that they had any quarrel with each other because of faith.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what period exactly, in the Middle Ages? Are we talking about the 10, the 11th or the 12th century here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the 10th and the 12th, all the way until after the Turkish occupation.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There aren't any quarrels so to speak between the populations except for minor wars between the various feudal leaders, but the crusades, when the crusades go to Constantinople and Jerusalem and so on and so forth, we find that the Crusaders committed crimes against the local population. At the time then there is this religious factor that comes into play in the conflicts, but that's a factor that is -- that is exterior to the region as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You just said two untruths, Mr. Tomic. The first untruth was that there was a clash between Serb Orthodox and Catholic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. I never said that there was a conflict between Catholics and Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I heard from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tomic has addressed it, but we would object to Mr. Seselj's characterisation of the witness's testimony as untruth. That's for the Bench to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be up to the Judges it to decide, but in order to decide they need to be in possession of all the evidence, of all the elements. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there any time when there was what conflict between Serbs and the Crusaders, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when the Crusaders crossed the Balkans, there was violence against local populations. It's not something I studied in detail, but quite possibly the Serb populations fell victim to such actions at that time, but there were also meetings between the Crusaders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I find that apparently the Crusaders may have committed criminal actions according to you. And in case that indeed happened, why? Why did it happen? Did these -- were these action committed for religious reasons or for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for religious reason maybe, but also for -- to loot the local areas or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean that the Crusaders might also have been looters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I read about that period, yes, they sometimes committed such actions in the Balkan region.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I'm drawing your attention to the fact that the witness is only speculating about this. He has no evidence that Serbs ever clashed with the Crusaders. He's just speculating, guessing. He said so himself a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you know that the Crusaders' attack on Byzantium helped Stefan Nemanja to make the Serbian state independent of Byzantium?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed at the time during one of the Crusades, there was a meeting was Stefan Nemanja and Baba Hosa [phoen] of course there were several crusades. I'm not a specialist in the matter of crusades. But I know that it happened. Violence was committed against the local populations, and it's quite possible that at some point these people shared the same political objectives. It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, the witness is not talking about any kind of confrontation between the Crusaders and the local Serb population. He just mentioned some crimes that may have been committed by these people whilst they were crossing the area. That's what I understood from what he was telling us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, the point is that the expert has no historical data to corroborate what he's saying. History has recorded that the great Serb bishop Stefan Nemanja met Barbarosa at his court. He extended hospitality to him and his army, and he used the Crusaders to free Serb completely of Byzantine power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned that meeting but it was only during one of the crusades. There were several crusades during the Middle Ages and they were quite different. They did not happen in exactly the same way every time, but once again this has nothing to do with the topic of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm aghast at the level of your education. You seem to practically know everything about everything. But the witness has just told us that this was not part of his report, his review, and he may give answers on some areas but not on everything. So you have to think in terms of your own interests. Do you want to continue in that direction, or would you like to highlight for us, the Judges, significant elements that would enable us to better understand the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question to do with the Middle Ages, and I believe it's very important. In fact, two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first is do you know, Mr. Tomic, how Byzantine writers treated Bosnia? Who is it, in their opinion, that populated Bosnia? Whose little state was it?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about the 10th century, on -- based on the document of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, at the time the Caslav, the Serbian state extended to the current territory of Bosnia. And these were the Serbian populations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Kinnamos, an important Byzantine writer? What does he say about Bosnia? Who lived there?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He talks about Serb populations living under -- on one of the banks of the Drina River and in Bosnia as well, but what he also says is that these populations, the populations living in Bosnia have their own customs. He suggests then that there are differences between them and the other Serb populations living on the other bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in terms of religion, in terms of their faith, these populations living in Bosnia, what was their religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia was part of the -- all the bishopries, Catholic bishopries at the time. Of course it's evolved throughout the centuries, but this region was mostly under the influence of the Roman Catholic Church. At the time, we talk about the Bosnian Catholic church, and it seems that this church varied or was quite a bit different from the Catholic church at the time. There were differences. It was seen as heretical at the time, but once again, I'm not a specialist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put a very specific question to you. Was there a single mosque in Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not because you had to wait until the 15th century, the second half of the 15th century to see the beginning of the Ottoman Empire in the region. In 1462 or 1463 Bosnia became part of the Empire, and at the time there was no Islam or Muslim faith in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the time before 1462, Bosnia was Serb, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia was either integrated into Serb states or other states, but as I said, the boundaries kept evolving, changing throughout the Middle Ages, because there's a country that we haven't mentioned much that's Hungary, and the Kingdom of Croatia, at the beginning of the 12th century was integrated into Hungary, and Hungary played a major part. Hungary tried to expand its boundaries towards the south of the region. Hungary played a major part in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before talking about the influence of Hungary, before Hungary incorporated these Bosnian territories, my question is the following: Was Bosnia then -- was Bosnia Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there was both Serb and Croatian influence in the current north-west of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's a region where you had influences coming from Serbia, from the east and from Croatia or Hungary to the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but apart from the so-called state influence, if I could say so, of course the states were not the same as the ones we understand now in the modern sense, but what we are interested in is the following: The people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's quite difficult because we don't have a census. They're -- they're feudal states, you know, and there were documents produced by the feudal states, so we can work on these documents. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, those who lived in Bosnia at the time, did they have -- did they speak Serbian? Was their language Serbian? What about their religion, culture? I'm not mentioning the influences, you know, as my fellow Judges mentioned, influences which are influences from the states as we see them now, but regarding their culture, their language, were these people -- let's take an example. People living around Sarajevo at the time, were they really different from those who lived around Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well -- well, Belgrade was always within the boundaries of the Serbian state in the Middle Ages, so it's not a good example, I believe. However, a Bosniak state will be set up in the Middle Ages and will start existing in the Middle Ages, and one of the late last kings of Bosnia, Tvrtko, was crowned in the Orthodox tradition in reference to the medieval Serbian state. But I believe that in this area there are influences, all sorts of influences, Western as well as Eastern. But I remind you I'm not a specialist of the Middle Ages. I'm not an historian dealing with the Middle Ages. I haven't studied all available sources regarding this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, these questions that you're getting both from the accused and the Judges, I'm sure you see the purpose of all this. The question, of substance in the end, you know, is to know whether at the very beginning, in the origin, Bosnia was Serb or not, without taking into account the various influences that may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the sources that we have of that time dating back, it is mentioned as being a Serbian region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Another issue is important to me, and I'm glad the witness now confirmed that Bosnia according to his contemporary sources Bosnia was Serbian, all the sources agree under which archbishopry was Bosnia in the 11th century and onwards? That's a very important question. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I know that there was a rivalry between Dubrovnik and Bar and Split, and I know Bosnia was integrated into the archbishopry. If Dubrovnik was the seat of the archbishopry, I know at one point in time there was a redefinition of the limits of the archbishopry. So it's either Bar or Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know some of these things, and you guess others. Isn't that correct, Mr. Tomic? The Dubrovnik archbishopry at one point encompassed a number Serb territories, but when was the Bar archbishopry set up, do you know?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's in the 11th century but I don't know exactly. I remind you this is not my speciality. But this was a very important element for each King, you know, to have a religious structure next to the political structure in order to cover the territory that was controlled by the King. JUDGE ANOTNETTI; Yes, but at the time and in the Middle Ages in Europe, wasn't political power under the influence of religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, at the time, power did come from God; so there tends to be a very great importance given to everything religious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said something correct a moment ago, namely in 1777, the Roman Pope crowned Mihailo Vojisavljevic, son of Stefan Vojislav to be Serbian King, you know that; but you don't that know ten years earlier the Pope established the Bar archbishopry in 1767 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the 11th century I had forgotten the exact year but I know at the time there was a will, the kings of Zeta wanted to have their own archbishopry they no longer wanted to depend from the archbishopry at Romnic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be an error on line 3 and line 6. It's not 1767, it must be 1067 and 1000 -- it must be 1077.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know which territory the Bar archbishopry covered when it was established?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it covered the territory of the state of Zeta as it was at the time and encompassed Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say probably. So you're not sure. But you were correct. You don't know all of it, do you, that it encompassed Duklja, Travunija, the Hum land, and Bosnia. You gave a partial answer, but it's correct. What was the official title of the Bar archbishop?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that his official title was Primus Serbia? You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you surely ignore that the current Bar archbishop is also Primus Serbia by official title although he's an ethnic Albania?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... aware of this data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had you dealt with the Serb history in greater depth, you would know that. Mr. Tomic, as you erroneously stated here that the Serbian state came into being, that it originated in the region of Rasa and you said that it spread towards the south, Kosovo and Macedonia as it developed. From whom did it take these territories, from what state?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on the Byzantine Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very good. At the expense of the Byzantine Empire. But what people lived on the territory to which the Serbian state spread?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were Slavs and in the south Greek and Albanian, but that's in the southern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you ought to know that according to Constantine Porphyrogenitus only two Slavic people came to the Balkans, the Croats and the Serbs. There are no third people, Slavs, right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many more Slav tribes at the time, you know, but some did attract attention more because probably they were more powerful or more organised than others, but in the 7th century the Byzantines recorded a few tribes. The Slavs went all the way down to Saloniki and each area had the name corresponding to each tribe so there was quite a variety than what Constantine seems to hint. But then after maybe there was several tribes that came together. Serbs and Croat tribes sort of managed to attract around them other Slavic populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why are you mixing up peoples and tribes? Don't you know that the Serbs had more than one tribe when they arrived in the Balkans? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there could be several Serb and Croatian tribes, but there could also be other tribes that were neither Serbs nor Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there are no historical sources referring to those other tribes, only to Serb and Croatian tribes. Isn't that correct? There is no historical source showing that any other Slavic people apart from the Serbs and the Croats arrived in the Balkans. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Slavs settled in Bulgaria. They became Bulgarians, but at first, you know, Bulgarians originated from Asia Minor. They spoke Turkish but -- and there was a mix between these people coming from Asia Minor and the Slavs. So these Asians became Slavs so at the time we're not talking about Croats or Serbs you're just talking about Slavs. What is called the Slavic invasion in the 6th and 7th century doesn't only deal with the territories that will become Yugoslavia later on. It also deals with the rest of the Balkans, the other side of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Tomic, what two great Serbian tribes inhabited Macedonia? What are the names of those two Serbian tribes that settled there?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You haven't heard of the Mijaci and Brsjaci, that those were two Serbian tribes that settled in Macedonia? You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. As you're a linguist --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a linguist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You studied Slavic languages as far as I know at University, at that institute. Are you aware of the various dialects of the Serbian language, the main ones?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... study languages at first but then very quickly I oriented myself towards history, so I didn't go into linguistics for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are various dialects, Stokavian, for instance. In all this area a distinction between made between various ways of speaking. Stokavian, Cakavian, or Kajkavian with variants for each of these dialects. For instance, Ekavian, Ljkavian, and there are various subcategories, subsets within one given dialect or area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As your knowledge of this is insufficient, I will ask you whether I would be right in saying that Serbian, that is Stokavian, consists of old Stokavian, middle Stokavian and new Stokavian. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I happen to have read this. This is not unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that old Stokavian is spoken in present-day Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that middle Stokavian is spoken in the Prizren and Timok parts of Serbia and that it is referred to as the Prizren Timok dialect?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not study linguistics in this respect, at this level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But you have heard of new Stokavian; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying this new Stokavian is divided into Ekavian, Ijkavian, as to standard languages, and Ekavian as a non-standard dialect?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I read something to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, didn't you have to know this if you wanted to write a serious report on the idea of Greater Serbia, especially an idea linked to an ideology on which I have imposed a personal stamp?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language dimension was mentioned by me for the 19th century. For instance, in the writings by Vuk Karadzic. At the time, it was a dominant idea in -- among the Slavists. Be there from Cekjar [phoen], from Slovenia. They're associated the Serbian nation with those who spoke Stokavian. But this definition was provided by intellectuals and did not rely necessarily on the real identity of the individuals living in those various areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we're now dealing with very specific and very complicated issues of linguistics, and judging by your questions it seems that Ekavian was the non-literary, spoken language. All the things you say cannot be challenged by the witness nor confirmed hundred per cent. What do you want to establish in putting those questions? What do you wish to show to us? Could you in one question to the witness help us understand what you are trying to show us? In this way everybody would save time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. President, I wish to prove to you that this witness is absolutely incompetent to testify as an expert on these issues. For him to be an expert in this trial his knowledge of these issues would have to be greater than mine. If I am a full-time professor we would need an eminent member of the academy here who would say he says this, this, this, and this and, that's his ideology. Yet here is a man who is hardly qualified to be an assistant professor, and he knows nothing. That's what I want to demonstrate to you. He's worse than Oberschall. He knows nothing about anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But regardless of that, there are things that he knows. For instance what he wrote about the 19th and 20th centuries. Now as part of your Defence you want to argue certain things. For us to be able to understand your approach, you need to ask questions that help us understand what you try to establish. I may be wrong, I may be right, but I believe I understood that initially you wanted to demonstrate that Bosnia was initially Serb. Now, as to the language, you seem to demonstrate that in those areas there are supposed to be Serbian or "Greater Serbia." All these people at the time used to speak a language that was from the literary point of view the Ekavian or an everyday language Ekavian. Is that what you want to show? If that is so, put the question to the witness and he can say, "I agree," or, "I don't agree with you."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite like that, Judge. My view is that all Stokavians are Serbs and the witness knows that the greatest Slavic scholars in the world advocated this standpoint in the 19th century. Let me ask him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've heard of Joseph Dubrovski a Roman Catholic abbot Slavic scholar; Safret [phoen] and Kopitar, Jernej Kopitar. Did all three of these greatest Slavic scholars of the 19th century consider that all Stokavians are Serbs, that Cakavians are Croats, and that Kajkavians are Slovenes. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was indeed what the Slavists of the time thought. Those who spoke Stokavian were according to them Serbs whether they be Orthodox, Catholics, or Muslims. But this was a standpoint established on the knowledge of the time. Later on, however, various national identities materialised and focused on other criteria, not just a language one. Those who spoke Stokavian among the Catholics are going to identify as Croats and not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's do it step-by-step. You were answering a question and you said something important. Those who spoke Stokavian, were they regarded as being Serbs? You seem to say that in the 19th century this was not challenged. Those who would speak Stokavian were Serbs. Is this what is to be understood by your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a matter of fact we're speaking about Slavists who are going to define national identities, but this does not mean that the people involved, the populations were asked for their matter. It's a definition from the top down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but back in the 19th century you have individuals. The names are to be found on line 2, page 33. These people seem to say that all those who speak Stokavian are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the prevailing view among the Slavists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the prevailing view of the Slavists in the 19th century. You agree on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least this way we can make headway. 1830s, 1840s, 1850s. This is confirmed then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We're going to try to make headway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now we're coming to the 20th century. Do you know who Aleksandar Belic is? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he played some part during the First World War, because he was an historian, but I can't remember right now, but indeed it rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The name is familiar to you, but you don't know that he was one of the greatest Slavists of the 20th century; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the 20th century. I'm not a linguist. I can't tell you as an expert. You have to ask this of a Serbian linguist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you don't know that Aleksandar Belic was also the president of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know all the names of the presidents of the Serbian science academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have never heard of Belic's greatest work, Slavic linguistics in two volumes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I never studied linguistics. I studied languages. I studied Serbo-Croatian at the time, that these were language courses. We learned grammar, vocabulary, but we did not have any advanced linguistics courses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that the science of linguistics goes to the very heart of languages and makes it possible to determine the origin of language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know some facets of linguistics when they are linked to the national question, but it was not necessary for me to go into each and every detail of this science. There was a definition of the Serb nation on the basis of the Stokavian dialect. This was an important data in my view, but it was not necessary to go into every detail of this question. I know that at some point in time there was a definition of the Serb nation on this criterion and that was enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know, Mr. Tomic, that Aleksandar Belic proved that the Stokavian or Serbian language belongs to the east Slavic group of languages to which Russian, Ukrainian, bellow Russian, Bulgarian and present-day Macedonian also belong, whereas Cakovski [phoen] as the Croatian and Kajkavian as the Slovenia language belong to the west Slavic group of languages which includes also Polish, Czech, and Slovak. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not now how I was introduced to Slav languages. I was spoken to about eastern Slavic languages, Russian, Belorussian, Ukrainian, and then you had eastern central languages and -- eastern as it were. So besides Serb, Croat, but also Bulgarian. So these are the three main families that were introduced to me that I'm aware of. I never heard of any association of Serb or Serbian with Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, then, Mr. Tomic, how come I can understand everything a Russian says and I can't understand what a Pole says? Isn't that odd?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sometimes understand Polish people. There are many common words in Slavic languages. They may be pronounced a little differently in Polish. "Mleko," milk is the same in basically all the Slavic languages. So if you make a bit of an effort you manage to understand each other after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course there are many words I will understand, but when a Pole speaks to me in Polish I don't understand him, right? I need an interpreter for Polish; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Polish is a bit more difficult because there are a lot of "Chur" and "CH" sounds. It is much easier for a Serb to understand a Czech or a Slovak rather than a Pole. Of course for a Serb it is easier to understand a Bulgarian or a Russian. The Polish case is a specific because you've got all the nasal sounds and therefore you may not have that sounds to such an extent in other central and eastern Slavic languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, put your question so that we understand what you're trying to demonstrate. We realise that there are three families of Slavic languages. What are you trying to demonstrate? Oh. The witness says there are three families. You say there are two. Just try to have us understand what you're trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are there two or three families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told that there were three families. That's what I was taught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are three in your book and two in the accused's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry, but I, too, learned that there were three families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Seselj, apparently there are three families among the Slavic languages. You are of the view that there are two. Can you, through a question, try to prove this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to avoid wasting time questioning the witness, I can tell you. When Yugoslavia was created, political measures were taken to create a third South Slavic groups of languages, but linguistics shows that this is untenable. In linguistics there is the eastern and western group, but now I've come to the place where Mr. Tomic deals with linguistic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mention here the agreement between a number of Serbian and Croatian intellectuals from 1850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. I'm being told that we have to have a break. Your associates seem to be here, and they should be coming into the courtroom later on. We are going to have to explain to them how computers work, so apparently we're going to have a 30-minute break. Indeed during the break they can be told how to push the various keys so that also they understand how computers work. In other words, we shall resume at quarter past 4.00 in the presence of your associates, and I'll ask them to introduce themselves before you go on with your questions. Let's reconvene at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible can they come and see me for five minutes before that? I have to see them before they show up in the courtroom, because I don't want to mess things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The hearing is resumed. I'd like to welcome the associates of Mr. Seselj, and I would like to ask them to introduce themselves one after the other. Please give me your names. Let me start with the one sitting on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, my name is it Zoran Krasic, legal advisor to Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MS. RAGUS [Interpretation] I'm sorry about this. My name is Marina Ragus, case manager for Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Aleksandar Vucic, legal advisor to Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JERKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Slavko Jerkovic, legal advisor to Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As I said, I wanted to welcome you to this courtroom. I'm sure that you were shown how these computers you have in front of you work. If at any point in time you have a problem, please notify us and the usher or registrar will come to your help. We're now going to proceed with the cross-examination. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you stated that a number of Serbian and Croatian intellectuals met in 1850 and agreed about a unified literary language. Where was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly where it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thus you don't know that it is the name of the venue that gave the name to the agreement in Serbia and Croatian linguistics, and it's quality the Vienna agreement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you mention it I remember, but it just escaped me a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know what literary language the Croats had before the Vienna agreement?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the years 1830, 1840, in the Slavonian and Croatian territories various languages were used. The official language for quite some time was Latin in the Croatian parliament. German was also widely used in Zagreb. It's called Agram as well under its German name, talking about the city of Zagreb. And in the years 1830 to 1840, the movement of -- the national movement is called Illyrian. That's the way the language used at the time is also called, and the actors of this Illyrian movement decided to adopt the Stokavian language in their publications because many more people used to talk that dialect than the other two. Kajkavian or Cakavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, in which language did the Illyrian movement start to publish its books, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljudevit Gaj. He spoke German. His German was fluent. He spoke German fluently. And amongst the most influential people in that movement Ijekavian was the prevailing language, but very quickly they decided to adopt the Stokavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in which areas was Kajkavian spoken?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas where Kajkavian was spoken were the areas around Zagreb, roughly, but if you look at the map to see where these -- where Kajkavian was spoken, it goes up to Sisak, if I'm not mistaken, remembering the maps I've seen, the maps where you see where Kajkavian, Cakavian, or Stokavian were spoken. But usually it's the districts around Zagreb that are defined as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If you know that Hungary as it was then was divided into counties and Croatia was part of Hungary, in what three counties was Kajkavian spoken?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Zagreb itself, and I don't remember the names of the relevant administrative units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that those were Zagreb, Krizevac and Varazdin counties? You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not remember, but, yes, indeed these were the three regions. But if I remember the maps I reviewed in various books dealing with that issue, the area went beyond the area where Kajkavian was spoken, went along these three Zupanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the first half of the 19th century, did Croatian national consciousness exist in any way in Slavonia whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time if you look at the current territory of Croatia, the same territory was divided into various parts. On the one hand you had Dalmatia. Dalmatia came under the authority of Vienna. And then you had Croatia and Slavonia that came under the authority of Budapest. These territories were divided. They would later become part of Croatia. At the time there was no real Croatian identity because the areas where the Croatian population lived were divided. There was no national identity amongst all these populations. In Dalmatia people would see them receives as Slavs. It's only in the second half of the 19th century that the Croatian and Serb nationalities started to come to the fore, but in Croatia and Slavonia faster, it went faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who led the systematic imposition of Croatian national consciousness in Slavonia in the second half of the 19th century?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, since in the first half of the 19th century Croatian national consciousness did not exist, it had to be implanted in some way. Somebody brought it into Slavonia if it did not originally exist there. Who brought it there?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whom you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you should know that those were Joseph Strossmayer and Franjo Racki. Do you know what their main theory was and how they managed to Croatise Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two individuals are part of the Yugoslav movement in Croatia. They spoke -- they spoke in favour of the Serbian and Croatian getting closer in the political and cultural areas. Strossmayer and Mihailo, the Prince of Serbia, came together, and at the time they decided that Serbia would become part of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a first stage, and the second stage of this cooperation would be an association between this state of Serbia and Slavonia and Croatia at the end of the '60s. That's when it happened. Strossmayer and Franjo Racki are major players in this thing, in the formulation of the unification of Southern Slavs. Strossmayer set up an academy of science, the Yugoslav academy of sciences where this project was given shape.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I need an extension of an hour, because this expert keeps wasting my time answering questions I don't ask. I ask him, for instance, what the main theory of Strossmayer and Racki was and he tells me the whole story of the two of them which is partly correct more or less, but he doesn't answer the question. Now I have to repeat it again in order to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've identified a problem here. Mr. Seselj is asking you who was at the beginning, at the origin of Croatian national consciousness in Slavonia. Your tell him that you don't know. Then he gave you the names of Strossmayer and Racki. Then you told him that you knew these two individuals and that they worked in favour of the Croats and the Serbs getting closer or together. It seems to me that it's not exactly what the accused was expecting. That may explain why he's slightly irritated to see that you do not answer his question. Could you please give us some more information about the role played by these two men in terms of the Croatian national consciousness in Slovenia, or would you confirm that these two men were not advocating the Croatian national consciousness in Slovenia, not at all, but that they were advocating the bringing of Croatians and Serbs closer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To answer your question, let me say that historians recently, starting in the 1990s and up until now, some historians believe that these two men wanted to Croatise the populations, to convert the Orthodox Serbs to Catholicism. That was a hidden agenda, however. That was never publicly proclaimed. Therefore, it's quite difficult to work on that basis, on the basis of such an allegation, because we have a lot of documents from these -- these intellectuals, from their circle. And since -- since apparently -- if they had this hidden agenda but if they never publicised it, what can we say about it? But I believe that this allegation was made in a book about the history of the Serbian people, a book publishing by Duskan Pospavelic [phoen]. In the chapter dedicated to Strossmayer, that's what's said about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you also spoke about the role played about these two men in the attempts made to unify the Slavs from the south. When you talk about unification here, was it a Croatisation or a Serbianisation? I don't know exactly what word I should use. I hope that you get my point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time Strossmayer was more interested in the cultural area, and he was -- he would leave to the Serbs what was related to the political area. But also you have to take into account the situation at the time. At the time the idea was to unify the Serbs in the Empire, Austro-Hungarian Empire, or to unify them with Serbs from Serbia. The project as -- varied depending on the political situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There have, Mr. Tomic, you don't know that the main theory of Strossmayer and Racki was that Serbs and Croats are one single people, that the Catholics of that people are called Croats and Orthodox oriented ones are called Serbs, but they belong to a single people.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, this was an opinion that prevailed because some say that Serbs is -- Serbian is the same as Croatian. I'm talking about the languages. It was called either Serbian or Croatian. At that time, people believed that Serbs and Croats were very close to each other and that they were a part of the same nation, that they were one, same nation, and that was the view adopted by Djuro Danicic, a Serbian intellectual. He worked together with the Yugoslav academy of sciences founded by Strossmayer. Djuro Danicic wrote dictionary of the Serbian language or of the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1857 it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about Strossmayer? When did he write his book?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1850, 1860, 1870. He became part of the political life, because he was a member of a popular party, the Narodna Stranka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To summarise, the main thrust of Strossmayer's ideas was that the Serbs and the Croats were part of a single people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He indeed believed that they were very close to even other, these two peoples. But when you start studying this ideology, then you realise that basically this is a plan of unification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how can you square the circle? If the Croats were Catholic and the others were Orthodox, how can you unify them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe at the time religion wasn't seen at the time as something that would divide people. Focus was made on something that would bring people together. That was language. So this is a population that lives in the Austro-Hungarian empire and that is trying to get as much an autonomy within this empire. So either you could have a third entity within the Austro-Hungarian because it's divided into two part in 1867 and the purpose, the objective of the political forces in Croatia at the time was to obtain maybe a third entity within the empire that would have brought together all southern Slavs. That was one of the scenario possible. The other one that had been envisaged was the following: Depending on the relationship that local power in Croatia could have either with Budapest or Vienna, then it could possibly unite with Serbia. But this idea that Serbians and Croats weren't single people is not an idea that you find only with these two people in the 19th century. It's very widespread. Until World War I, many intellectuals believed that this was one single nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this nation is based on language, not on religion since there are different religions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There are differences, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's one of the main element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this concept at the time, you know, in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, isn't this an attempt to unify, to create this third entity without having any regard to the differences in religion in order to create an entity that would fit within the empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Strossmayer would rather have autonomy for an entity that would bring together all southern Slavs from the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question but -- okay. I do understand this cultural unification and this movement for this, but did they support themselves? Did they back themselves on common writers, common works of literature? So did they consider -- did they take into account what the Croats and the Serbs had written and the writings of these two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when Vuk Karadzic re-established the Serbian literary language, then there was an agreement to say that this was Serb or Croatian. That was in 1850. And then the authors followed the advice of and the recommendations of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you could say that this was very -- this is very artificial. But before this actual operation there were writers, and did people think that they were represented either by one or the other writer from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't really gone into this. I haven't really studied this in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I have to skip over a lot of my questions, because you are intensively wasting my time. You are speaking here of the Serbian cultural club --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, when you dealt with this question, what exactly was your point? Could you give us another question so we could understand what your point is and what your case is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried, Your Honour, but the witness is not responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formulate a question that could summarise your case, and then he will say either yes or no, or I do know or I don't know. At least we'll know.
