The Bench will understand what your question is, we'll have a trace of your question, and we'll be able to understand really what your point is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take another path in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Yugoslav academy of art and science in Zagreb published five volumes of private correspondence between Strossmayer and Racki?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were collections of what they have written. I don't really know the exact date of publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a collection of letters. It's not their collected works, which were never publish. Are you aware that from their correspondence it is evident that their basic idea was to use the Yugoslav idea to get all the Serbs to convert to Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not studied in detail the political action of these two people, but I know in Serbia Vasilije Krestic highlighted this phenomenon. However, I haven't looked into this in detail, but I know this is the conclusion he reached in his work. This is an historian who research the history of Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is Vasilije Krestic today one the greatest living Serb historians?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it's an historian who works in the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. However, I don't know to what extent he's recognised by the community of all historians in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an historian you ought to know that. Have you heard of Slavko Gavrilovic, another member of the academy?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have never even heard of Slavko Gavrilovic a member of the academy who dedicated his whole life to studying the life of the Serbs in Slavonia and Serb-Croat relations. And who spread Croatian national consciousness in an organised manner in the second half of the 19th century through Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a politician called Pavinovic, who played an important role. At first in Dalmatia there was a popular party that was created Narodna Stranka that brought together Serbs and Croats. At the time it was the Slav identity that was dominant in that area. But then Pavinovic really defended the Croatian national interests and there was a split between Split -- between Serbs and Croats from that moment on in the party, in Narodna Stranka when Austria arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When Bosnia-Herzegovina became occupied by Austria, there was great divergence of opinion between Serbs and Croats within this Narodna Stranka and Divnovic supported integration of Bosnia-Herzegovina into Croatia and Slavonia. But the creation of national identities and the consolidation of national identities only occurred after 1860 -- 1870, interpreter's correction. And in the late '70s, then there was the split and creation of a specifically Serb party in Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was Mihovil Pavlinovic [phoen] by profession?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that he was Roman Catholic priest?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in that party, among the Serbs and Catholic representatives, there were also clerics who were involved in political life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here you deal with the activity of the Serbian Cultural Club, and you list the names of certain eminent intellectuals who were members of the club. You say that the members of the club periodically gave lectures on different topics. In your view, was every lecture of every individual member of the club something that expressed the standpoints of all the members of the club?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On what basis did you describe the lecture of Vaso Cubrilovic on the movement of Albanians, on moving out Albanians as the jointly held standpoint of all the members of the Serbian Cultural Club?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me that from the moment when a good number of conferences were organised on the same topic which was nationalisation of different regions like Kosovo and Vojvodina, and when we're talking about nationalisation, here there's a reference to population transfer, forced population transfers. Then in the spring 19 -- as of -- in the spring of 1937 there were a good number of conferences on the same topic, so it seemed that the Serbian Cultural Club did not disagree with what was discussed with -- in the framework of these conferences. The fact that there were so many conferences does not mean that the solution that is envisaged to solve the question of national minorities is disregarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are we -- what time period are we talking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1937.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Are we talking about society of nation? But there were populations movements under the auspices of the League of Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, Vaso Cubrilovic was the secretary of the Serbian Cultural Club. He's not an outsider or just a member. He was on the board. So what he said had a lot of weight, just because of the position he occupied. He was secretary general of this Serbian Cultural Club.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any other member of the Serbian Cultural Club at any time express in public his agreement with the ideas that Vaso Cubrilovic put forward in his lecture?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find any trace that would make it possible to say that such-and-such -- that the point of view of such-and-such could be confirmed or denied. But as I said, you know, when I started testifying, there was also an official policy going in that direction, which was to reduce the weight of national minorities in Yugoslavia. So at the political level you have convergence, and you also have this convergence within the Serbian intellectuals regarding these -- what to do with the national minorities. In 1938 the Yugoslav government signed an agreement with the Turkish government on the -- on the transfer of 200.000 Muslims to Yugoslavia. This was not materialised, never came to anything, but there were a number of conferences in 1937, for example, Djoko Perin, and Perin published what had been lectured in conference what was a brochure and he wanted to distribute this to all members of parliament at the time. So there was this will to really pressurise politicians at the time in order to -- through recommendations, but the Yugoslav government was -- wanted -- was -- was of that opinion, you know, to try and reduce the weight of national minorities in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction it was not to Yugoslavia but from Yugoslavia to the Muslims that move.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where was this standpoint formulated in the Serbian Cultural Club? You say it was the standpoint of the Serbian Cultural Club. Where was this formulated? Nowhere; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe the formulation is a bit awkward, but these positions were not challenged at the time. As I said, you know, they were repeated over and over. And these opinions were also repeated after World War I, because some intellectuals who were members of the Serbian Cultural Club joined the Ravna Gora Movement with the same ideas in mind. These were ideas that were moving around, you know, in that -- in those circles. They were not necessarily developed in the journal of the Serbian Cultural Club.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is only one man who gave a lecture on the transfer of Albanians. That's Vaso Cubrilovic. And then you claim that his ideas were accepted by all the other members of the club, although the standpoint was nowhere formulated, the members nowhere expressed their opinion, and it was not confirmed in the Official Gazette of the club; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one person who mentioned this, Djoko Perin also. I know this topic of nationalisation of some of the regions was discussed in a number of conferences. I believed that since the topic was studied under different frameworks, it meant that there was agreement on the solution envisaged to solve the problem of national minorities. Now, of course if you read Srpski Glas, the problem is that Srpski Glas as a newspaper was only issued two years later. It started being published two years later in 1939, in November 1939. So I'm talking about conferences that were held in the spring of 1937, and we don't have any echoes of those conferences in the journal of the Serbian Cultural Club. If the journal had existed at the time maybe these conference would have been dealt with in the journal. But there's a shift in time here. There's a time lag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think this is incredible, Judge. You see, he's not answering my question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was Djoko Perin?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was an engineer in agriculture in Sarajevo. I -- this booklet exists. I looked at it. It was in a national library of Serbia. He's mentioned in the work of Ljubodrag Dimic, an historian, who devoted an entire chapter of his books to the Serbian Cultural Club.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The name Djoko Perin might be a pseudonym, Mr. Tomic, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw Djoko Perin on the booklet, on this brochure, and I found it also in the study by Mr. Dimic. They seemed to contain information to the effect that he was from Sarajevo. His identity was specified on the brochure and he's even mentioned on the front of the brochure. It was said that it had been published for the MPs of Yugoslavia and senators of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... agree that he was a very marginal intellectual whom nobody knows anything about or almost anything?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious that he's not one of the main intellectuals in the Serbian Cultural Club. He doesn't have the same reputation as Jovanovic or Dragisa Vasic, the president and vice-president respectively. He doesn't have the same profile at all, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So public speeches by two men, Vaso Cubrilovic and a non-entity, Djoko Perin, are something that you identified with the policies of the Serbian Cultural Club without any foundation whatsoever and without any evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the only one who arrived at this conclusion. Most of the researchers who looked at the Serbian Cultural Club did see what kind of solution was put forward in order to resolve the issue of national minorities. I'm not the only one to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who else arrived at this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in mind the chapter in the book by Ljubodrag Dimic, in the history of cultural policy in the first Yugoslavia and in the inter-war period in three volumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In his book does Ljubodrag Dimic claim that the Serbian Cultural Club as a whole wanted to transfer the Albanians out of Yugoslavia? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may not have used those terms, but he did mention the national programme and all the ideas that could actually make up a national programme as they circulated within the Serbian Cultural Club, including the idea of displacement of these populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're falsely ascribing this to Ljubodrag Dimic; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian Cultural Club wanted there to be a Serb unit established once the Croatian Banovina had been established. That was the gist of what he advocated. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, this club was founded in January 1937. So the initiative was probably started in December 1936. The idea of creating a Serb entity within Yugoslavia only arose in August 1939, because in the spring of that year, until the summer of that year 1939 there were negotiations between Dragisa Cvetkovic, the head of the government and the leader of the Croat Peasants Party on setting up a Banovina in Croatia. Only when this Croatian Banovina was established in August 1939, only then was there a reaction by the Serbian Cultural Club with a specific claim, which was to establish a Serb entity. Since there was a Croatian entity, they wanted -- a Croatian entity, they wanted a Serb entity within Yugoslavia. So that is two years after this organisation was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the members of the Serbian Cultural Club were almost all Frankophile of a liberal orientation, that they were all intellectuals and democrats, and there were many Freemasons among them? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. At the time if you want to look into the composition of the movement you cannot say of it that you would be fascist movement like they were also at the time. Indeed often its members are in favour of liberal democracy. But this being said, one of the main points put forward by the Serbian Cultural Club at the time is that the foreign influence on Serbian culture should be limited. So even though many of the intellectuals in that club studied abroad, for instance Slobodan Jovanovic, he studied in Switzerland and in France. There was a will to basically only rely on Serbian national cultural values, limiting the influence of Marxism, of artistic movements or trends such as futurism, say the modernist trends of the time. But I would not indeed say of that organisation that its part of the organisations that really got more and more numerous in Europe. This is late 1930s. Like fascist-type organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are transposing things in the -- on the cultural scene, which is the wrong place. You forget that the main orientation of the Serbian Cultural Club was to oppose Marxist and fascist trends that were coming from abroad. Marxism and Fascism were considered by them to be equally dangerous enemies.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm actually referring to articles I was able to read in Srpski Glas. Mention was not made of fascism, but the members of the club were not in favour of Fascist Italy or Nazi Germany at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... fascism I also mean the Nazi ideology. Nazism in the first place, perhaps. Were they all committed anti-fascists as became evident in the war that followed?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer for all but for a good part of them they later -- some of the leaders were involved in the government in exile or in the Ravna Gora Movement, which was indeed was a resistance movement at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it the case that the establishment of Banovina Croatia was done constitutionally?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the 1920s there had been a claim on the part of Croats for autonomy within Yugoslavia, and this question was an impediment to the good functioning of democracy at the time, so much so that there was an assassination in the Assembly of Yugoslavia, which led to a proclamation of dictatorship in 1929. So the Croatian question did cause tensions within Yugoslavia, and it took almost 20 years before a solution was proposed to meet the specific claims and demands of the Croat parties at the time. Now, as to whether they complied with the constitution, I don't know, but the powers at the time, we were close to war, this was 1939, and it was important to resolve the Croatian question at all price so that Germany or Italy would have no pretext for intervening. There was a need for the largest unity possible in Yugoslavia in order to face the looming threats at the time. At the time, we were in August 1939, a lot of things have already happened in the area, happened in Austria and Czechoslovakia so there is this threat looming on the Yugoslav authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which constitution was in force then?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 1931 constitution, which was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did this agreement violate that constitution?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this agreement put into question the way the country was organised administratively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... prescribed by the constitution?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the -- every detail of the Yugoslav constitution, but this agreement challenged the administrative organisation of the country as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you have dealt here with the Chetnik Movement, and you mentioned the assassination of the Croatian political leader and president of the Croatian Peasants Party Punisa Racic in 1928 in the national assembly.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I made reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about Bogdan Krizman?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Croat historian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One of the greatest Croatian historians of the 20th century, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question, but he published numerous works.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that his father Hinko Krizman was a deputy in the National Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbs, Slovenes and Croats?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you know that Bogdan Krizman in one of his works describes how his father had told him that priest Korosec president of the Slovene popular party and Minister for Foreign Affairs had warned previously his deputies who were sitting in their chairs in the parliament behind the deputies of the peasant party to sit somewhere else that day?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that detail that I never saw in all the books I have written about the history of Yugoslavia in the inter-war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's because you haven't read very valuable works, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that's what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard about Vaso Kazimirovic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across this name, indeed, but I couldn't tell you right off the cuff who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Therefore you don't know that Vaso Kazimirovic published a history of Yugoslavia between World War I and World War II in four volumes?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that he, too, refers to the testimony of had Hinko Krizman? You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know this detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If you had known then you would have drawn the conclusion that minister Korosec knew in advance of the assassination attempt at Stjepan Radic and probably organised it himself?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have reached page 38 where you say that Punisa Racic shot Stjepan Radic in the national assembly. It's 38 in Serbian. I have to go faster because I have no time for all the questions I want to ask of you. But I am finishing with this issue, and I'm moving on. You stated here that the democratic party, too, between two wars had its own Chetnik organisation. The radicals had one and the democrats had one. The Chetnik organisation of the democrats was led by Kosta Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers have to make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is indeed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... assume when pauses are observed. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. Do pause before you answer because not everything is recorded. Please answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember that specific detail still. Kosta Pecanac would create Chetnik units when the war broke out in Yugoslavia, and he decided to collaborate with the Germans and was in fact opposed to the Ravna Gora Movement. Besides some of the men who fought within the Chetnik units will move to the Ravna Gora Movement later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned in the examination-in-chief that the word "Vojvoda" means "military leader"; correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned "military leader."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the difference between an army Vojvoda and a Chetnik Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this word was used in Chetnik units, which are irregular military units mainly waging guerrilla war, but "Vojvoda" the term was used to speak of senior officers of the Serb army. You had Vjovod Putnik during World War I, for instance. Now, I couldn't tell you the whole history of the use of that word "Vjovod" to qualify members of the Serb army staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're telling us something that might be relevant. You told us that this word could also be used, the word of "Vjovod," could be used to qualify senior officers of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During World War I, Vjovod Putnik Micic was used. It was a term used in the army to be found in most of the books dealing with the history of World War I. But now -- there we were talking about the regular army, but that word was also used to qualify irregular units. For instance, in early 20th centuries, as of 1903, there was an organisation sending Chetnik units to Macedonia. This organisation equipped itself with an Executive Committee in Belgrade, and it was that committee that appointed the Vjovods of the units to be sent -- to be established in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know which rank was equivalent to Vojvoda in the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: General, but a five-star general.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know about a French general who became a honourary Vojvoda of the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- when, in the 19th or in the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time of the First World War. A very famous French general.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Might have been Franchet-d'Esperey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Franchet-d'Esperey. He was a marshall, too, a five-star general.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Yes, indeed, general or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a marshall, which in the French army means a five-star general. He got the same title in the Serbian army. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it mentioned, but that would not be surprising given the collaboration between the French and Serb armies at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give the name of that marshall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you spell it out for it to be in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Franchet-d'Esperey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Unlike the army Vojvoda, Chetnik Vojvoda was not a rank. It was a title; correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the Chetnik Movement, to these irregular forces, the rules of appointment may have been different or may have differed depending on the various constellations. I know that early 20th century in the Chetnik Movement where the field of action was Macedonia, the title was decided by the Executive Committee of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you go on, Mr. Seselj I'm told by the registrar that you still have an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Chetnik Vojvodas even before World War I and later could have the title of Chetnik Vojvoda and the army rank at the same time?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes indeed. Some of the Vojvodas who were-- fought in the irregular Chetnik forces were also officers of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Major Tankosic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vojislav Tankosic is indeed one of the main Vojvod.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How about Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes he was also known as Vjovod Vuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Chetnik Vojvoda; right. You do know something, Mr. Tomic. And do you know that in World War I -- World War II there were Chetnik Vojvodas who never commanded any Chetnik units?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite possible that Vojvodas or people who were -- were called as such before the war started, it's possible that these people did not join the ranks of the Ravna Gora Movement. The Yugoslav Army in the homeland. The historians who studied this do not see a direct link between the Chetnik Movements of the inter-war period and the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am asking you about the Ravna Gora Movement. Were there any Chetnik Vojvodas who never ever commanded any Chetnik units?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Vojvoda Dobroslav Jevdjevic? Is he one of those that never commanded any Chetnik units?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobroslav Jevdjevic was one of the Chetniks who was active in one of the Chetnik organisations in the inter-war period together with Ilija Trifunovic Bircanin. He was active in Dalmatia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Judges, I'm asking one question and the witness is replying to another. He's using up my time and he's not answering. I'm asking him about World War II, the Ravna Gora Movement and whether Dobroslav Jevdjevic as a Chetnik Vojvoda ever commanded a Chetnik unit and he's telling me the life story of Dobroslav Jevdjevic and what he did between the two world wars. How am I supposed to get out of this vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that he played a major role in the wars that I mentioned I don't know if he was head of a unit but I know he played a major part in terms of cooperation with the Second Italian army. At that time in that particular area of Dalmatia and Herzegovina, the Italian army was occupying the territory, and the Italians had decided to support the Chetnik, and Dobroslav Jevdjevic was the main contact of the main interlocutor of the Italian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know, I hope, Mr. Tomic, that the Ustasha right away in 1941 committed atrocious crimes against Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that the Italian army, as soon as it heard of those crimes, came to the rescue of the Serbian people trying to save them?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Italian army intervened to help the Serb refugees who were fleeing before the Ustashas and the crimes they had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Italian army, after its General Staff learned of these crimes, decided to reoccupy the Independent State of Croatia in its own zone of interest?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in May 1941 there was an agreement with the Ustasha authorities in Zagreb with respect to the occupation of part of Dalmatia by Italy. The idea was to define what areas would be occupied. But I'm not aware of anything related or any plan related to the total occupation of the independent Croatian state that at the time included Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not aware of anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something that I do not quite understand. In 1941 you had the Italy, Germany, all these countries together, and apparently the Ustasha were on the side of the Germans. Am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They enjoyed the support of the Germans, but before the war they were supported by the Italians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in 1941 they were also together with the Germans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Germans and the Italians but the Italians at the time wanted to secure the territories they thought should come back to them in Dalmatia along -- along the coastline, and for them the Croatian state was an obstacle to their objectives in the region. That's why they decided to call on the Chetniks in order to counter the objectives of the independent Croatian state. The situation is rather paradoxical. You have Italy that is supporting the Ustasha power in Zagreb in 1941 but very quickly there is a high level of mistrust that appears between the two parties and the second Italian army then supported Serbian civilians in the areas it occupied, and the army, the Italian army, supported the Chetnik Movement, armed the Chetnik Movement and used the Chetniks to fight against the Communist resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was very complex indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are trying to shed some light on this situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation. Judges, I would like to explain to you briefly because I want this to be clear to you and everyone else as well. The Ustashas and Ante Pavelic will emigres in Italy. After the Marseilles assassination attempt against King Aleksandar, Pavelic was tried in France in absentia. He was convicted to death. And Mussolini refused support to Ustashas and isolated Pavelic. Pavelic was a prisoner in Italy and his main Ustasha leaders. Only in 1941 does Mussolini let them leave Italy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We object to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you object? Mr. Seselj is trying to shed some light on the situation for the Judges, because the Judges may be confused by this situation where three or four parties come into play. So what do you base your objection upon?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It appeared to the Prosecution that Mr. Seselj was testifying, and I believe the Court had already admonished him in that regard and that was the basis for the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I get your point, but we need additional information, and I believe that it's indeed very relevant for us to find out that Ante Pavelic was detained in Italy to be then set free. So, please, Mr. Seselj, complete your explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, it is precisely the Croatian historian Bogdan Krizman who wrote in five volumes the history of the Ustasha movement. It's very objective and acknowledged in the world. In Zagreb the Ustashas put themselves in the service of Germans, whereas Italians withdrew from their occupation zone to the territory of Italy. Zadar was Italy. They also held some other towns that were directly annexed to Italy. The Ustashas had a free-hand in their own territory and that's where the manslaughters began. After those slaughters Italians renew the occupation of one part of the Independent State of Croatia to save Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, please. This is all very interesting, but the way you should clarify all this is by putting questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had just started to do that. I was about to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that the reason, Mr. Tomic, why Chetniks started cooperating with the Italian army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I let you answer, Mr. Seselj has given us some data, information. Please answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They first had contacts where -- with the first wave of refugees from the areas where massacres had been committed. Then depending on the region, for example in Montenegro, cooperation between Chetniks from Montenegro and the Italians started after the conflict between the Chetniks and the Communist Party in Montenegro. Contacts between them occurred in Montenegro but in Dalmatia as well, and in the Lika region, part of the Krajina region. Contacts was different between them depending on the region where it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And was it the same in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of Herzegovina was occupied by Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Italian army returned there only after the Ustasha crimes. Isn't that so? At one point the Italian army had left Herzegovina. Am I right? And then the crimes happened. You don't know these things, do you? Okay. I'm moving on to another question. I'm not going to insist. So we agree that the Chetniks of Draza Mihajlovic cooperated with Italians. Do we agree that the reason for that cooperation was that Italians were helping Chetniks defend the Serb people from Ustasha crimes? And the second reason was that Chetniks were helped to fight Communists?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- corresponds to what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the cooperation of Chetniks with Germans, apart from the traitors that Draza liquidated himself like Pecanac? Did Draza or any of his commanders cooperate with Germans?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Draza Mihajlovic and some German officers had contacts in 1940, but nothing followed up. But during the war at some times there were contacts between enemy factions or -- which were enemy on paper. At some point the Communists got in touch with the Germans asking them not to attack them in 1943, because they were in a weak position or an unfavourable position, and their point was as follows: They told the Germans in Zagreb that the Communists were not attacking the German forces but mostly the Chetnik Movement. So as you can see, during the war negotiations took place sometimes and of a very surprising nature between warring factions that should have been opposed to each other but times they get in touch and they have discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But isn't there another reason for that at the time? Was there a pact signed between Germany and -- by Germany and Russia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We're talking about 1943. The occupiers, the Germans, the Italians, and the Chetniks had attacked the Communist Resistance Movement. They needed some time off the fighting, and they had asked -- had asked a truce from the Germans. Yes, but indeed the situation in the war is extremely complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My question was -- you have wasted my time needlessly. Do you have evidence of Chetnik cooperation with Germans apart from some sporadic negotiations to exchange prisoners and trifles like that? Do you have evidence of any important agreements between Chetniks and Germans about military cooperation?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was cooperation with the Italians but not with the German armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. I would love all your answers to be as concise as this one. You mentioned those March negotiation. They were in Zagreb, right. Do you know that Tito sent three of his most important generals to conduct those negotiations in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a well-know fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Milovan Djilas, Koca Popovic, and Vladimir Velebit; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it written black and white in that agreement that the main enemies of partisans were Chetniks and they did not intend to fight the Germans? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. We need not spend any more time on that then. You state on page 42 that Draza Mihajlovic did not launch any important actions against the occupier; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was the strategy of that movement. After a number of actions again the Germans, retaliation was extremely violent on the German side, and they decided that it would be useless to provoke the Germans needlessly, and they decided to wait for the most opportune moment, i.e., the landing of the Allied Forces in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That Germans prescribed that for every one of their soldiers who was killed they would shoot 100 Serbs and for 1 wounded soldier, 50 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned it in the first part of my testimony during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... aware that the German occupying authorities gave a reward of a hundred thousand Reichmarks in gold to anyone who would help in capturing or killing Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware of any extensive Partisan action against the Germans? Before the end of 1944 when everything was over already?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the war started in Serbia, Communist Partisans attacked the Germans on a few occasions, but quite clearly throughout the following years it was more a civilian war between the Ravna Gora Movement and the Communists. It was more a war of that kind rather than a war against the occupying forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Tomic. Let's cut things short. Do you know how many SS divisions were formed by the Germans on the territory of Yugoslavia during World War II?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that they formed three SS divisions?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were some SS divisions that were formed with Albanians from Kosovo and Muslims in BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Kosovo there was the Skenderbeg SS division; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Herzegovina the SS Handzar Division was formed composing Muslim?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... name of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what third division was formed a SS division?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a Croatian division that was sent to the front to fight in the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. You don't know that Princ Eugen was formed out of volksdojcer, the German, I think, minority in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did encounter that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that that division committed the greatest crimes against the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vojvodina there were a lot of crimes that were committed against Serbs either by the Germans or by the military forces from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that that SS division, Princ Eugen was active on almost the entire territory of Yugoslavia as the Volksdojcer spoke Serbian so they were useful?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not studied the detailed role played by all these SS divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Croats established the Croatian legion comprising 10.000 soldiers and sent it to the eastern front under German command and that it was broken up at Stalingrad?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a well known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're aware of that. There's a article by Stevan Moljevic from 1941 which you ascribe to the entire Ravna Gora Movement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that I explained what Stevan Moljevic wrote this in June 1941, he was not yet a member of the Ravna Gora movement. He joined this Ravna Gora Movement in August. However, this being said, he was appointed at the national Central Committee, and he was one of the main ideologists of this Ravna Gora Movement. So the idea that he developed in June 1942, he then defended those ideas with the Dragan Mihajlovic and within the movement of Ravna Gora. Most historians who study the platform of the Ravna Gora integrate this document into the national platform of Ravna Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For it to be a national programme someone had to make it official in the Ravna Gora Movement, not just historians. It's an individual act; right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are individual proposals. The Ravna Gora Movement is not a political party. This being said, even if this movement was linked to the Yugoslav government in exile because the armed forces of the Ravna Gora corresponded to the Yugoslav army in the homeland, the ideologists of this movement who were members of the Central Committee had political ambitions. The idea was to set up a new order within the Yugoslavia that was to be after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to have a break, we will break for 20 minutes and after the break, the registrar will tell me how long Mr. Seselj still has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I can confirm to Mr. Seselj that he has 40 minutes left, but the Trial Chamber will give him no additional time. The accused had four hours. Four hours. This is all the -- this is all the questions of the -- answers to the question given by the accused and what the Judges asked is not deducted from this. So Mr. Seselj got four hours altogether. He still has 40 minutes and only 40 minutes. So please try and ask only very essential questions. Please focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you use Communist falsehoods here in an attempt to prove that the liquidation of Muslim civilians on the territory of Foca and the surrounding area by the Chetnik Pavel Djurisic was carried out with the aim of implementing ethnic cleansing. Are you aware that that crime was preceded by a heinous crime by the Ustasha which included many Muslims against the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- this is retaliation that occurred after massacres that had been carried out at the end of 1942. This being said, these are not forged documents or falsehoods. These -- recently in Serbia there was a debate as to whether or not the Chetnik Movement should be rehabilitated, and the text was signed by some 20 historians to protest against this rehabilitation and mentioned the number of 30.000 casualties for the period going from January to February 1943. In my report, I used the -- when I was using the conclusions of Jozo Tomasevic, I mentioned 10.000 victims. And Kosta Nikolic answered these historians, among others, you know, that there was an original of the operations carried out by Pavel Djurisic mentioning figures that were much lower than 30.000. And in the daily Vecernje Novosti of January 15, 2007 Kosta Nikolic is interviewed by a reporter of this magazine, Vecirnje Novosti. There's -- I think there's only one document, but the Antun Miletic and Vladimir Dedijer are two historians, you know, in one report you talk about 400 Muslim fighters and thousand civilians as casualties, and they believe that these two historians who studied this added one 0 to obtain 10.000, so there was just not one report but two reports and when you add the two reports that's how you come up with this 10.000. So Kosta Nikolic is an historian who made a dissertation on the Ravna Gora Movement, and he's one of the eminent -- most eminent -- eminently recognised historians in this speciality, and he contributed greatly to the rehabilitation of this movement and he's not taking that these documents are forgeries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you see how lengthy the witness's answer to this question was. Almost all his responses are as lengthy as this. You didn't want to extend my time. I take notice of this, but my cross-examination has been systematically sabotaged in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Madam, please put the front page of this book Mr. Tomic refers to, genocide against the Muslims in 1941 to 1945 by Vladimir Dedijer and Antun Miletic on the ELMO. Do we have it on our screens now? That's the book, isn't it, Mr. Tomic? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so given the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here now is page 31 of the preface to this book signed by Antun Miletic. The marked part, the last passage, please read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The most credible evidence of the genocide and crimes committed are the first and last names of 9.435 Muslims who were killed. If one adds to this number, the names of those mentioned in the documents presented, the number of dead is over 10.000, which is a contribution and monument to the Muslims who had fallen mostly on a genocidal basis. This is the only way to arrive at the truth. The effort is not in vain because the victims deserve it."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dedijer and Miletic are highly respected historians of a Communist provenance? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Antun Miletic is a colonel and a Croat?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he's Croat, I can guess it. I didn't know that he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's still alive. He's now published volume four of his book on Jasenovac. He says as you can see here that throughout the war 9.435 Muslims were killed, and when one adds up everything, he allows that the number is over 10.000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the figures that are written, but it would be interesting to know what period is involved here. Is it 1943?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. As the title of the book says, it refers to 1941 to 1945. I assume you've read the book, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one of the book but it's a few hundred pages long and just a few years later I can't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is the preface to the book where Antun Miletic summarises and gives the overall figure.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have to read it. When you're talking about those 10.000 victims, you're talking January and February 1943. And there were other massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic --

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 1941 and 1944. There were other casualties. I believe this is a figure that only deals with January but maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... other victims. Where? You are lying intentionally, Mr. Tomic, aren't you, because you want to represent the Chetnik Movement as genocidal. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I'm saying in my report I said that the number of victims that fell to the Chetniks was much lower than those who fell to the Ustashas. I think I really made things very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And can you see from the previous passages that Antun Miletic also mentions the Muslims -- Muslim victims killed by Ustasha and the Communists and other Muslims? So this number does not refer only to Muslim victims of Chetniks but also of the Partisans, Germans, Ustasha, and everybody else who killed civilians. Isn't that clear from all this?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You show me a document, that's only an excerpt. I would rather give my opinion if I had the entire introduction. But Tomasevic, like others, basing themselves on the reports of Pavel Djurisic came up with a figure of 10.000 for the operations that were in -- that occurred in January and February 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're making this up. You're inventing this because you're a false witness, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, why are you saying that he's lying? It's easy. It's easy, you know, to say that and assert that, but give us reasons. On those 10.000, he's giving us an explanation. Either you like it or you don't, but this doesn't mean that he's lying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nota bene here there's a list. The victims were given names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, you put a question to me, and if you want me, I will -- to I will reply, but don't take it from my time. During the examination-in-chief and in his report, this witness referred to the book "Genocide Against The Muslims," and you can see from the title that the term genocide is being used in a political sense. It doesn't correspond to the legal definition the word genocide because we are where 9.435 Muslims have been killed in compared to 2 million Muslims that's not genocide but it's true that Muslims were killed that the Chetnik detachment of Pavel Djurisic killed Muslims is something I don't deny. I do deny that it had anything to do with Draza Mihajlovic and the overall policy of the Ravna Gora Movement. That's my explanation if you want one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so what can you answer to what has just been said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the archives that exist, and these are operations that were carried out after orders, and in the collection of work that was published in Yugoslavia, you can obtain in the archives the orders that were given early in January 1943 as far as these operations are concerned. This unit was under the command of Pavel Djurisic and was integrated into the Yugoslav homeland army, and the command of this unit was in Montenegro at the time. We're talking here between spring 1942 and spring 1943. The command was around Kolasin, and this unit was operating around Kolasin. So there is a geographical closeness between the command of the units -- and the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, how far Kolasin is from Foca?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but it's close. It's mountainous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that that is an area that's impassable, that you need even today almost an entire day to reach Kolasin from Foca? Are you aware that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that it's mountainous, and it's -- maybe there aren't many passes. I haven't been there. But the two areas are close from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Ravna Gora Movement of Draza Mihajlovic conducted a policy of brotherhood between Orthodox, Muslim, and Catholic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Draza Mihajlovic, not in 1941 and 1942, but during the war he did talk to the Croats and the Muslims. But when you look at all the documents, you know, articles in the press of the different units of the Ravna Gora Movement, notably in the Ravna Gora journal, the one called Ravna Gora, that the idea to have a Greater Serbia within a Greater Yugoslavia is the main idea, and to expelling all non-Serb from it. Then since the Ravna Gora Movement was in a difficult situation in the midst of a civil war, it couldn't just, you know, have everybody on their back, all the non-Serbs fighting against them, antagonising all non-Serbs, which is why they approached the Croats and the Muslims, since the Communist Partisans were able to attract these -- these Croats and Muslims into their ranks. So I would say this is -- this is something -- the Chetnik Movement was faced with a difficulty and that was the way to bypass it rather than wanting to really attract Muslims and Croats into the Ravna Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the vice-president of Draza's national committee was a Muslim leader Mustafa Mulalic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are two people, the one you just mentioned, and Isman Popovac [phoen]. These were two Muslims, members of the Ravna Gora Movement, but they were very marginal. I mean, there weren't that many Muslims in the Yugoslav homeland army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many were there, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Few thousands, I believe. Potentially there were 360.000 men that could be mobilised in -- to join this Yugoslav homeland army, but the real combatants that had weapons were much less, some 30 to 40.000 only. Therefore, I don't believe that there were that many Muslims. You know, a few thousands, but they were in a minority compared to the other -- the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Chetnik commander Zvonko Vuckovic, who was a Catholic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this rings a bell, but I can't give a detailed answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that he was one of the closest collaborators of Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've encountered that name, but I can't give you more elements on his biography. I do know he was close to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that he emigrated to America after the war and published his memoirs there?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, but I don't know this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Chetnik commander Nika Bartulovic from Dalmatia, a Serb of the Catholic faith?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also encountered that name, and it's true that in Dalmatia there is a Trifunovic Barcinan who set up a committee bringing together Serbs and a few Croats all with Yugoslavia in mind. So it is true in that area there were Croats, but they were defending a Yugoslav political framework and -- but they did take part in the Ravna Gora Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Vojvoda Momcilo Djulic in the Dinara Chetnik Division had two battalions of Serb Catholics from Primorje?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were several units, because his Dinara Chetnik unit was made up from existing units in Western Bosnia and in Lika or north Dalmatia, Northern Dalmatia, but I've never seen anywhere mention of two battalions that would be specifically made up of Catholic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And yet you are prepared to take it for granted what the Communist falsely said about the alleged crimes committed by Djujic.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was speaking about the victims, I realise on official documents established by the commission who was in charge of establishing war crimes. For instance, the Dinara Chetnik unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Igor Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finished my answer. Current answer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You haven't heard of Igor Grahovac. Igor Grahovac is a Croatian historian who established and recently published in Zagreb, Croatia that in World War II a total of 2.900 Croats were killed by Chetniks. That means Ustasha killed in battle, perhaps members of the Home Guard, civilians, any kind of Croats. The total number is 2.905. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of his work but I can say that the Dinara Chetnik unit was located in an area where Ustashas did not go to. They were called by the Italians who would have made sure that the Croatian armed forces could not penetrate that territory. So the main actions carried out by the unit were geared towards the forces of the Communist Partisans and the number of casualties that was established refers to fighting against the Partisan forces attacking villages where there were Communist Partisans, including in Western Bosnia. So there was no direct confrontation between that unit and the Croatian population, because they were in a so-called free territory with Italian support until September 1943, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of a single large-scale Chetnik crime against Croatian civilians?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia at the time was part of the independent Croatian state, so there were Croatian victims for -- especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina but not in Croatia as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fighters among the victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, fighting and less fighting so, because in this context of a civil war, we've seen this, it does happen that civilians be targeted by one or the other army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a very precise question. Do you know of any large-scale crime, something that would have struck the public opinion at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding Croats, no, I have no recollection. I didn't look so much into that maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you did know how to condemn en bloc wishing to ethnically cleanse Muslim and Croat territories. You seem to have studied here also some of my speeches and writings, and you quoted from them. Is it correct that from one programme to another and in many of my public appearances there is constant repetition of one political goal, page 78, achieving full national, spiritual, economic, and political unity of the Serbian people, as well as mutual understanding and solidarity between Orthodox Serbs, Muslim Serbs, Catholic Serbs, and Protestant Serbs. Does that occur very frequently in my platform documents of the Serb radical right party, the Serbian Chetnik Movement and my writings?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was often repeated, but there are very few Protestant Serbs. As to Muslim Slavs, who would declare themselves or identify themselves as Serb, there were very few as well. In 1948 when there was not yet a Muslim nation, there were some 70.000 Muslim Slavs that had identified themselves as Serb, so this is a very small number. And there are also very few Catholic Serbs. So to here highlight this aspect of the solidarity, why not. But indeed as to the number of people who would identify themselves as Catholics or Serbs, numerically speaking there are not very many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it obvious from my public appearances that in principle I'm not very much interested in how people declare themselves. All Stokavian Catholics I consider Serbs and all Stokavian speaking Muslims I consider Serbs.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indeed your vision of the Serbian nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how could I then advocate the expulsion of people whom I believe to be Serbs of other faiths? You mentioned my speeches during my tour of the USA that were nationalist by nature.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that I was there and my travel was organised by the Chetnik organisation of Vojvoda Djujic, but you don't know that my official sponsor was the Serb National Academy Vuk Karadzic from Cleveland.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I got a multiple entry American visa valid for one year with an unlimited number of entries and exits from the USA?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you sent several months in the United States, that you went there on several occasions because you -- as of the time when you could have a passport. That is only after 1986. Only then did you get a passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the mayor of Cleveland, George Vojinovic, now senator, handed me ceremonially a certificate, an award for human rights?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but as I said, when I was answering the Prosecution questions, at the time when you were a dissident of the Communist regime many human rights associations, organisations in Europe and the US had defended you at the time of the trial in 1984. So this approach does not contradict all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious that my ideology was the same now only they are a bit more developed now my views.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say in the early 1980s your ideas were not developed in the same way as they were in the late 1980s. There was a development. It was more systematic, and your writings were going more in depth on the issue of the Serb national question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but when you say end of the 1980s, that's 1989. That's the year of my tour of America.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially think of 1988, 1989, and 1989, because when you toured in the US, you set forth a political programme, in fact, a political programme for Serbia, and beyond that for the Serbian people living in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that at the time of my visit on the building of the Cleveland Senate the state flag was hoisted and that award was given me after that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in Washington I was received by the then-minister for war veteran issues, Edward Darwinski?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I was received at the State Department?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I was received also by a group of senators and members of the House of Representatives at the US Congress?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... know these things. Therefore, my ideology was not questioned by the US authorities as long as I was an anti-Communist. It became question when I opposed the American policy in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that there is a lobby, tradition, and practice in the US, so it's easy to meet with members of the Congress or the Senate, especially when you have people who are of Serbian origin that can facilitate the talks, but that doesn't mean that official power or government approves. It is a practice that was studied by researchers in sociology. It's this lobby practice, lobbying practice in the US.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I never said they agreed with my ideology, but I was not a questionable personality because of my ideology, regardless of lobbies, not everyone can meet with an American minister, or congressmen or senators.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how this institution functions, but it's easy to get in touch with members especially if you champion political and less political causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the US President Harry Truman was posthumously decorated General [as interpreted] Draza Mihajlovic with one of the highest decorations in the US, legion of Merit.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that it was only two years ago that this decoration was handed to Gordana, Draza Mihajlovic's daughter?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would American President Truman have decorated a war criminal as Communist -- Communist painted Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well the Americans did not conduct the same policy towards the Ravna Gora Movement. At least they did not have it all the same position as their -- as Great Britain, which ended up giving up that movement in 1943, but it is a fact that Draza Mihajlovic was decorated after World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your expert report, you lied when you wrote that Vojvoda Djujic stripped me of my title of Vojvoda, and you have never seen a document that would be a foundation for that claim.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied on an article that was published in the daily Vecernje Novosti that seemed credible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means if we took everything that was published in the newspapers about me and took that into account, I would be worse than Hitler.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say so, but it seemed to be reliable inasmuch as Vojvoda Momcilo Djujic had shown that he was not satisfied with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know why a clash occurred between me and Djujic? Not because of my cooperation between socialists. Do you know the real reason?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that this was an opposition regarding monarchy and cooperation with former Serb Communists in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever found any writing of mine or a speech in which I speak positively of monarchy as a form of rule? You could have only found passages where I say the people have the right to decide whether they want a monarchy or a republic, but you could never have read anything written by me speaking well of the monarchy.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in your programme you speak about the monarchist tradition which has to be entertained, but it doesn't mean that you were advocating monarchy in Serbia because you gave a choice to the Serbian citizens saying that a referendum could be held, but you were very critical towards Aleksandar, the prince who was heir to the throne from the Karadjordjevic. You thought that the national cause would make an equation between Ustashas and Chetniks. And I found many statements showing this point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What matters to me is that you never found any passage where I praised the monarchy as a phenomenon. Mr. Tomic, you probably know that the Serbian Radical Party supported the decision of the Belgrade authorities to return to the Karadjordjevic family their old court and to allow them to live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was indeed envisioned by you, but that doesn't necessarily mean, and you said so expressly at the time, it didn't mean all the same that monarchy should be restored in Serbia. There is a difference between the two. It's one thing to authorise the family to get their property back, and it's another thing to restore monarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you don't know that the conflict between Vojvoda Djujic and me occurred when Djujic sent Dr. Milos Prica, an American Serb, to Belgrade to become my main political advisor?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that in my first contact with him, I realised Dr. Milos Prica was an American spy and rejected any possibility of him becoming my advisor?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I relied on the information published by the press. I relied on your own might writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If you had read my books more carefully you could have found that in several of my interviews, but you didn't.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that after that Vojvoda Djujic got Milos Prica, Ana Mitrovic, and some other American Serbs to go to Biljana Plavsic to become her advisors?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you don't know that those people talked Biljana Plavsic to betray Republika Srpska? You don't know that do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic is now in a Swedish prison convicted of war crimes, while Milos Prica, her advisor is now the ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations in New York. You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Biljana Plavsic is in Sweden, but I do not know this gentleman Milos Prica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You could have heard only one thing, that Vojvoda Djujic, in one of his statements to a Belgrade television called Studio B, said that he would strip me of my title of Vojvoda and attack my verbally. And that television crew was sent by Vuk Draskovic, who then held power in fell grade.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was a television channel controlled by Vuk Draskovic and the movement for Serbian renewal. I saw some interviews of his in the Nin newspaper in Belgrade. There were other interviews or reports in the press related to differences between you and him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vojvoda Djujic, under American pressure, had to say that, but he never stripped me of my title of Vojvoda. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the United States brought pressure to bear, but on several occasions in the Serb press he expressed his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there is no official document stripping me of that title? It simply doesn't exist anywhere.

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a ceremony, but, yes, indeed I don't think there is a specific document related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the ceremony never took place anywhere, did it?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nice. You see, Vojvoda Djujic died at the age of 90 something, but he was obviously in full possession of his mental capacities, and he had partially to give in to US pressure but not completely. Is that correct, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: YVES TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer and say anything related to any pressure exerted by the US authorities on this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, will I have at least until 7.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because you've used up all the time that had been allocated to you. If you have one last question, you may ask it, because I don't know, the Prosecutor may have additional questions. If you have one last question to put to the witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask two if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First, Mr. Tomic, you lied when you said that unofficially the Socialist Party supported me and additional elections for deputy from Rakovica. That's page 89 in Serbian. Correct? That they supported me unofficially by giving me free access to official media. That means that it's a natural and normal situation when I have no access to the media, only that is normal.
